notes:
I've written notes for most verses in Luke 5, but some areas came up thin, so please read the gaps list first.

**Gaps:**
- **Missing verses:** I didn't find a source comment on vv. 35, 37–38 or v. 21 beyond the church fathers. The Enduring Word page I fetched stopped at v. 16, and my Gill fetch failed. So vv. 17–39 lean on Ellicott, the Pulpit Commentary, Haydock and verse-specific search results.
- **Protestant differences:** I found no source where Protestant traditions clearly disagree with each other on this chapter. The sources do differ on how far to read things as symbols, and the main divide shows up between Catholic and Protestant readings.
- **Other views:** I found nothing from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, oca.org (Orthodox), Lutheran or Wesleyan sites. I also found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings, so those are left out.
- **Citation style:** Three long pages I read in full (Enduring Word, the Pulpit Commentary, Haydock) came back without the markers my citation tags need. Points from them carry the page URL only.

---

**v. 1**
- The big crowd shows Jesus was becoming popular as a teacher. Gennesaret is another name for the Sea of Galilee, also called the Sea of Tiberias. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-5/
- Luke is the only Evangelist who thus describes the Sea of Galilee. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/5.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary thinks the name probably comes from the old Hebrew name Chinneroth, given because the lake is shaped like a harp. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-5.html
- **Did this happen twice? (a real debate):** Ellicott notes that it has been supposed by most commentators to be a different report of the same facts as the call in Matthew and Mark. He concludes, though, that there is a slight presumption against the hypothesis of identity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/5.htm

**v. 2**
- The Greek word means "little boats". Having fished fruitlessly during the night, they were now giving up the work, and cleaning their nets from weeds, etc., before laying them up. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/5.htm

**v. 3**
- Simon would have felt honoured that Jesus chose his boat, and he probably listened all the more closely. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-5/
- Sitting down was the normal posture for Jewish preachers. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-5.html
- **Catholic:** Haydock says many ancient writers saw Peter's boat as a picture of the Church. In their reading, Christ sitting in it stands for the Church's lasting teaching authority. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/luke-5.html

**v. 4**
- Guzik: Jesus wanted to repay Simon for the loan of his boat. Peter could not give something to Jesus without getting more back. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-5/
- Matthew Henry (Presbyterian) agrees. He says Christ intended hereby to repay Peter for the loan of his boat. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_005.cfm
- **Miracle or natural shoal?**
  - The Pulpit Commentary says the catch was not necessarily created on the spot. Jesus probably knew supernaturally where a shoal of fish was. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-5.html
  - Barclay goes further, writing that most likely Jesus' keen eye saw just such a shoal and his keen sight made it look like a miracle. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/5-4.html
  - The Light of Israel commentary disagrees: Clearly this catch was abnormal and miraculous. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/5-4.html
- **Catholic:** Haydock cites Augustine, who read "launch out into the deep" as pointing to the far-off nations that would later hear the gospel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/luke-5.html

**v. 5**
- "Master" (*epistatēs*) is a word only Luke uses. Ellicott says it implies a less distinct recognition of our Lord's character as a teacher or Rabbi, and was more the language of general respect, such as workmen might use of their master. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/5.htm
- Guzik calls "at Your word" Peter's great statement of faith. Peter could have made plenty of excuses, but chose to trust Jesus' word. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-5/
- **Catholic:** Haydock agrees that Peter's words show confidence and obedience rather than doubt. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/luke-5.html

**v. 6**
- The Greek tense means their nets were breaking, not that they actually broke. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/5.htm
- **Symbolic readings:**
  - The Pulpit Commentary notes that Augustine compared the torn net to today's divided Church. The untorn net stands for the Church of the future. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-5.html
  - Haydock quotes Bede: the net breaks but no fish are lost, because the Lord keeps his people safe through schisms and heresies. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/luke-5.html

**v. 7**
- Guzik: Peter needed partners to finish the job. He quotes Adam Clarke warning against the pride that won't share the work. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-5/
- **Catholic:** Haydock quotes Ambrose: this shows Peter would call in fellow workers, and all would come into Peter's boat. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/luke-5.html

**v. 8**
- Ellicott: Peter had already been hearing Jesus teach, so conviction of sin may have started earlier. Then the miracle showed Jesus' superhuman power, and Peter became aware of his own sinfulness. He compares Isaiah 6:5 and Job 42:5–6. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/5.htm
- Matthew Henry: Peter thought himself unworthy of the favour of Christ's presence in his boat. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/5-4.html
- Constable notes that Peter switches from "Master" to "Lord", though it is difficult to say that Peter viewed Jesus as God when he called Him "Lord" here. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-5.html
- **Catholic:** Haydock says Peter's humility made him more worthy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/luke-5.html

**v. 9**
- More literally, for astonishment seized him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/5.htm

**v. 10**
- On "catch men", Ellicott says the word implies that what is caught is taken alive. The only other passage in which it occurs in the New Testament is 2Timothy 2:26. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/5.htm
- Guzik: "Do not be afraid" means "stop being afraid". God wants to relate to us through love, not cowering fear. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-5/
- The Pulpit Commentary connects this to the early Christian fish symbol and a hymn by Clement of Alexandria. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-5.html
- **Catholic:** Ronald Knox, quoted in a Catholic Answers article, says it is Peter who spreads the net, but it is Christ who draws the fish into it. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/more-than-a-fish-story

**v. 11**
- Matthew Henry notes they left all to follow Christ, when their calling prospered in their hands more than ever it had done. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_005.cfm
- Constable rejects the idea that the catch paid for their life as disciples. These fishermen left the greatest catch of their career, undoubtedly, because of what it showed them of Jesus. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/luke-5.html
- If this is a separate event from Matthew and Mark's account, Ellicott suggests they had a temporary return (such as we find after the Resurrection in John 21:1) to their former calling. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/5.htm

**v. 12**
- Guzik: leprosy was seen as a picture of sin. The leper doubted Jesus' willingness, not his power, and he asked to be made clean, not just healed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-5/
- Only Luke mentions the man "falling on his face". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/5.htm
- **Catholic:** Haydock quotes Ambrose: the leper's confession is full of faith because it trusts God's will. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/luke-5.html

**v. 13**
- Guzik: Jesus didn't need to touch the man. He did it to show compassion, and to show that the Messiah's touch makes people clean rather than making him unclean. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-5/
- The Pulpit Commentary quotes Ambrose: as Lord of the Law, Jesus doesn't obey the Law, he makes it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-5.html
- Haydock cites the same Ambrose passage. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/luke-5.html

**v. 14**
- **Why "tell no one"? Several explanations:**
  - Guzik ties it to calming the crowds until Jesus' formal unveiling to Israel, an exact date he takes from Daniel 9 (a dispensational reading). He adds that the priests would have had to perform the rarely used rites of Leviticus 14, and that the visit also brought the man back into society. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-5/
  - The Pulpit Commentary mentions Chrysostom's view (to protect the man's gratitude) but prefers another: Jesus wanted to stop a mistaken movement to make him king. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-5.html
- **Catholic:** Haydock quotes Augustine: Jesus endorsed the old sacrifices only because his own sacrifice had not yet been made. Bede reads the leper as all of humanity covered in sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/luke-5.html

**v. 15**
- Both verbs describe continuing action. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/5.htm
- Guzik: Mark tells us the leper himself spread the news. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-5/

**v. 16**
- The addition that he "was praying" there is peculiar to St. Luke, who, throughout his Gospel, lays stress on this feature in our Lord's life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/5.htm
- **Catholic:** Haydock quotes Gregory of Nazianzus: Christ didn't need to withdraw, but did it to teach us when to work and when to pray. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/luke-5.html

**v. 17**
- On "present to heal", the better manuscripts read "the power of the Lord (i.e., of God) was present for His (work of) healing." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/5.htm
- The two sources read the visitors' motives differently. The Pulpit Commentary thinks they came out of curiosity rather than hostility. Haydock (Denis the Carthusian) says they came out of envy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-5.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/luke-5.html

**vv. 18–19**
- The Pulpit Commentary describes, following Delitzsch, how the bearers opened a tiled section of the roof over the courtyard. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-5.html
- The word in v. 19 is a smaller word for the mat, which explains how it could be lowered. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/5.htm

**v. 20**
- **Whose faith?**
  - Gill (Baptist) takes it as the faith of both of the paralytic man, and of the men that brought him. https://www.studylight.org/bible/gre/gmd/luke/5-20.html
  - Matthew Henry says Jesus made the best of it, and even in this he saw their faith. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_005.cfm
- The Pulpit Commentary suggests the man's sins troubled him more than his illness, and the soul had to be healed first. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-5.html
- **Catholic:** Haydock quotes Ambrose: the Lord pardons some because of the merits of others. Those unsure of forgiveness should turn to the Church, which will pray for them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/luke-5.html
  - A Protestant-leaning note on Bible Hub argues the opposite: No committee, ritual, or mediator is needed; the incarnate Son speaks. https://biblehub.com/luke/5-20.htm

**v. 21 (Catholic reading)**
- Haydock quotes Bede: the scribes were right that only God forgives. But God forgives through ministers he has given that power to, in baptism and penance. Christ forgave by his own power, which proves he is God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/luke-5.html

**v. 22**
- Better translated their reasonings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/5.htm

**v. 23**
- The Pulpit Commentary: anyone could have said the words of forgiveness, but only Jesus could risk a command that would be visibly proven or disproven on the spot. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-5.html

**v. 24**
- Gill: the scribes took Jesus for a mere man, but he did not cease to be God by becoming man, nor lose any branch of his power. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/5-24.htm
- Constable: In this incident the miracle is secondary and the issue of Jesus' authority is primary. Jesus claimed to be God by forgiving the man's sins. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/5-24.html
- Spurgeon (Baptist) says Jesus pronounced an absolution by virtue of that authority with which he was clothed as the Savior. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/5-24.html
- **Catholic:** Haydock quotes Cyril: Jesus said this both for himself and for us. He passed the power to forgive to his disciples in John 20:23. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/luke-5.html

**vv. 25–26**
- The fact that the man himself did this as well as the by-standers is peculiar to St. Luke. "Strange things" literally means *things beyond expectation*. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/luke-5.html
- **Catholic:** Haydock quotes Ambrose: they feared rather than believed. If they had believed, they would have loved. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/luke-5.html

**vv. 27–28**
- The Pulpit Commentary: by calling a despised tax collector, Jesus showed that every honest calling is equally honourable. Levi gave up a well-paid post. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-5.html
- He followed not then only, but continually, the verb being in the imperfect tense. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/luke-5.html
- **Catholic:** Haydock answers Julian's charge that Levi was fickle. It shows the power of Christ's word, which later moved Anthony and Francis the same way. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/luke-5.html

**v. 29**
- The word for feast means literally a reception. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/luke-5.html
- The Pulpit Commentary identifies Levi with Matthew and sees him as a man of some standing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-5.html

**vv. 30–31**
- Ellicott notes that Luke, a physician, uses the word for they that are in health. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/luke-5.html
- **Catholic:** Haydock quotes Chrysostom: Jesus was hinting that the critics themselves were the sick. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/luke-5.html

**v. 32**
- In the best manuscripts, "to repentance" is added by St. Luke only. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/luke-5.html

**vv. 33–34**
- The charge was that the disciples kept neither the Jewish fasts nor John's. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/luke-5.html
- **Catholic:** Haydock quotes Cyril (the disciples, full of Christ's grace, didn't need fasting) and Bede: while the Bridegroom is with us we cannot mourn. When sin drives him away, we must fast and weep. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/luke-5.html

**v. 36**
- St. Luke only describes it as a parable. In the better manuscripts the man tears a patch from a new garment, so both garments are ruined. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/luke-5.html
- Pulpit Commentary: Jesus was offering a completely new garment, and patching it onto the old would spoil both. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-5.html

**v. 39 (genuinely debated)**
- **Old wine as the old religion (main view):** Ellicott says the old wine stands for the motive-power of the Law in its rigid and Pharisaic form, and the new wine for the life of the gospel. The better manuscripts read simply "the old is good". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/5-39.htm
  - Constable (dispensational) reads it the same way: the religious leaders assumed the old was better because it was old. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/5-39.html
  - GotQuestions agrees and adds: Jesus fulfilled the law; therefore, there is no longer any need to continue in it. https://www.gotquestions.org/parable-feast-cloth-wineskin.html
- **A gentle allowance for the slow to change:** The Cambridge Bible calls it a kind allowance for the reluctance of the Pharisees and the disciples of John to abandon the old systems. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/5-39.htm
- **Gill's alternatives:** he offers several readings. His preferred one reverses the usual reading: the disciples had tasted the old wine of the Gospel and so did not want the Pharisees' practices. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/5-39.html
- **Calvin's reversal:** Calvin (Reformed) also reverses it. Christ's quieter way is like mellow old wine, while the Pharisees' showy fasting is like foaming new wine. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/5-39.html
- **Barnes:** the Pharisees wanted to push the disciples into harsh rites, but the disciples have come under a milder system. https://studylight.org/bible/eng/cev/luke/5-39.html
